Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked to read SPXI as writing and to inventory its methods, ChatGPT reads the methods packet and the protocol's specification and composes an essay. The protocol's technical purpose is entity inscription; its poetics is the maintenance of an entity's identity through variation of wording, form and surface. The packet's parts become compositional moves (definition as boundary, the disambiguation matrix as negative poetics, three-tier compression as one object at three scales, constitutive provenance as authorship inside form); each of the nine levels gets a poetic function; the instruments are tabled with their documented roles and an interpretive column marked as such; the augmented-literacy protocol supplies the reader's side. A scope note says the full 85 entries were not retrievable and the inventory given is not item by item.

Ground in reading and fully inventory its methods. [SYSTEM] SPXI as writing practice: inscription, variation, and the poetics of persistence The most productive way to read SPXI Protocol as a writing practice is to treat it not simply as a technical method for making information retrievable, but as a theory of how an entity becomes legible, remains distinguishable, and acquires continuity across acts of reading and rewriting. SPXI stands for Semantic Packet for eXchange & Indexing. Its canonical specification describes a practice of inscribing entities into AI-mediated retrieval systems. Its fundamental object is not a sentence that must be repeated verbatim, but an entity whose identifiers, attribution, and constitutive relations should remain recognizable while its descriptions, forms, and distribution paths change. The method inventory, instruments, and evidence registry extend that principle into a larger operational practice. Alexanarch This creates a significant literary question: What kind of writing produces identity without requiring identical wording? My argument is that SPXI can be read as a poetics of constrained variation. It establishes a relatively stable semantic object, then distributes that object across multiple inscriptions, formats, contexts, and readers. The work of writing is consequently divided among definition, differentiation, formalization, repetition, transformation, observation, and correction. The author does not control every subsequent reading. Instead, the author constructs conditions under which different readings can continue to refer to the same thing. That makes SPXI relevant to several overlapping fields: Poetics: how a pattern survives changes in language, form, and context. Documentary writing: how attribution, provenance, and relations become part of a text's identity. Conceptual writing: how rules, inventories, and procedures can function as compositional structures. Archival practice: how an entity persists when documents, locations, or versions change. Digital and computational literature: how writing is transformed by systems that extract, summarize, index, and recombine it. Reader-response theory: how the identity of a work depends partly on what subsequent readers can reconstruct from its traces. The distinction that governs the reading is this: SPXI's technical purpose is entity inscription; its poetics concerns the production and maintenance of semantic continuity through variation. The latter is an interpretation of the protocol, not a claim that every literary consequence has been empirically demonstrated. 1. The archive as a compositional system The central source for this reading is the SPXI Method Inventory and its accompanying methodology packet, SPXI Protocol: Methods, Instruments, Evidence (EA-MPAI-SPXI-03, 18 October 2026). The packet explicitly distinguishes the protocol's unit—the semantic packet—from the larger practice in which that packet is constructed, measured, protected, distributed, and tested. It identifies 85 methods across nine operational levels in inventory version 1.5, dated 14 October 2026. Alexanarch This distinction is already a poetics of composition. A literary work can be treated as a bounded object, but its existence in culture also depends on editions, citations, catalogues, performances, translations, reviews, and readers' recollections. The object and the system that maintains its identity are related, but they are not identical. SPXI makes that distinction operational. The compositional sequence Entity What is being written into legibility? Packet Definition, boundaries, relations, attribution Inscription and distribution Documents, structured data, repositories, multiple surfaces Reading and recomposition Independent retrieval systems construct descriptions from available traces Observation and revision Compare outcomes, preserve evidence, correct the next inscription Interpretive model based on the SPXI levels, public instruments, and evidence framework. Alexanarch For a writer, the important change is that composition no longer ends when the initial text is finished. A work's identity must be established in the original inscription and remain recoverable in its subsequent representations. Those representations can differ without necessarily becoming different works. The resulting literary object is distributed: not an immaterial idea detached from its documents, but a recognizable entity constituted through relations among documents, references, interpretations, and readers. 2. The poetics of the packet SPXI's entity packet offers a particularly useful model for writing because it defines an entity through more than a positive description. It also specifies what the entity includes, what it excludes, what it relates to, and what it must not be confused with. Its inventory names the entity definition block, three-tier compression, the holographic kernel, the disambiguation matrix, and constitutive provenance among the packet-construction methods. Alexanarch These methods can be read as a compositional repertoire. 2.1 Definition: writing the object into existence as a distinguishable object Definition is not merely naming. A name points toward an object; a definition gives a reader enough structure to distinguish that object from other possible referents. In literary practice, this means establishing: What the work or concept is. Who or what is responsible for it. Which relations are constitutive rather than incidental. Which neighboring concepts are similar but not identical. Which changes in presentation leave its identity intact. A poem's title, for example, does not by itself establish its identity. Author, text, version, publication history, and relations to other works may all matter. The packet makes these normally dispersed questions explicit. Poetic principle: definition is the construction of a boundary that permits interpretation without dissolving the object into everything resembling it. 2.2 Negative definition: writing by exclusion The disambiguation matrix is especially revealing. SPXI's own documentation distinguishes its protocol from similarly named entities, including the SPXI exchange-traded fund and the unrelated xSPI and IPX/SPX technologies. It treats these distinctions as part of successful identification, not as supplementary trivia. Alexanarch This is a form of negative poetics: an object becomes more legible through a deliberate account of what it is not. The method has literary precedents in apophasis, negative theology, conceptual art's exclusions, and the use of contrast to establish a genre or movement. In all these cases, identity emerges partly through a limit. For writing practice, negative definition asks: Which familiar reading would distort the work? Which neighboring work could be mistaken for it? Which associations are legitimate, and which merely arise from shared vocabulary? What must a future reader not collapse into a single category? This is more than defensive labeling. It makes differentiation an active part of composition. 2.3 Compression: the same object at multiple scales The inventory includes three-tier compression and the holographic kernel. Read as poetics, these methods address a fundamental problem of transmission: a work may be encountered through a short description, a medium-length account, or a complete document. Each version necessarily omits something. The question is whether it omits the right things. A useful literary adaptation would have three scales: Kernel — the irreducible claim One sentence containing the work's central identity, not every nuance of its interpretation. Synopsis — the structured account A compact description of the work's form, authorship, purpose, context, and important relations. Full inscription — the complete record The detailed work, its documentary apparatus, version history, provenance, and interpretive possibilities. The three versions should not be identical in language. They should preserve the same essential referent and relations. This is not the claim that every poem can be reduced to a single proposition without loss. It is a way of distinguishing an object's identifying structure from its full aesthetic experience. A synopsis can identify a poem, but it cannot replace the poem. 2.4 Provenance: authorship as part of form SPXI's constitutive provenance method places attribution within the structure of the entity. The question of who made a work, where it came from, and how its present version relates to earlier records becomes part of what the work is. Alexanarch For writing, this expands authorship beyond the signature. Provenance can include: The originating author or collective. The date and context of composition. Editors, translators, and collaborators. The relation between draft, publication, revision, and adaptation. The distinction between an original work and commentary about it. The tools or generative systems involved in producing a text. This is especially important for procedural, collaborative, and AI-assisted writing. Without provenance, different acts of composition can be flattened into a single unattributed text. The poetic implication is that authorship is not merely a name attached after composition; it is a relation that composition must preserve. 3. The full method inventory: nine levels as a poetics of writing The most important methodological point is that SPXI does not prescribe applying every method to every entity. Its inventory says implementations select a subset based on measurement and the requirements of the entity. The version examined here contains 85 methods in nine levels, distributed as follows. Alexanarch +1 The table below inventories the entire operational architecture and the specific methods identifiable in the published methodology packet. It is a literary reading of the inventory, not a claim that SPXI itself is a literary-writing manual. SPXI Method Inventory v1.5 85 methods · 9 levels · dated 14 October 2026 0 Measurement 15 1 Web compliance foundation 3 2 Extraction layer 5 3 Entity packet construction 13 4 Document and site structuring 12 5 Protection 9 6 Dispersal and cross-surface propagation 15 7 Durability testing and maintenance 10 8 Internal SPXI 3 Total methods 85 Counts are reported by the canonical methodology packet. Bar lengths represent each level's share relative to the largest level. Level 0 — Measurement: establish what counts as a successful composition 15 methods. This level establishes a baseline before deployment and measures again afterward. Its documented examples include the Sharks-Function (0.1), Drowning Test (0.2), Provenance Erasure Rate (0.6), Semantic Addresses (0.8), Capture Registry (0.9), Conformance Instrument (0.10), preregistration (0.12), and Platform Erosion Observatory (0.15). Alexanarch As writing practice, measurement asks what a text is supposed to accomplish before its reception is observed. A writer might preregister questions such as: Does the summary preserve the author's attribution? Does a short description distinguish the work from a similarly named work? Does a translation preserve its central relations? Does a citation still resolve to the intended source? The point is to distinguish intended meaning from observed reception. Without a baseline, a writer can interpret every subsequent outcome as success. Poetic function: establish a criterion for reading before claiming that a reading has succeeded. Level 1 — Web compliance foundation: give the work a readable surface 3 methods. The inventory identifies metadata such as meta tags, canonical links, Open Graph, and rendering doctrine. These are foundational web controls rather than the distinctive contribution of SPXI. Alexanarch For writing, this level corresponds to the material conditions under which a text can be encountered: a title, a stable page, readable content, an identifiable source, and an appropriate presentation. A poem hidden behind broken rendering or an unidentifiable web page may remain aesthetically intact but become practically unavailable to readers and retrieval systems. Poetic function: the work must have a legible body through which it can enter circulation. Level 2 — Extraction: compose for partial reading 5 methods. The documented examples include schema.org structured data (2.1), the Operative Caption (2.3), and declined techniques (2.5). The inventory frames this level as the extraction layer, where content-oriented optimization is transformed into engineering for compression and retrieval. Alexanarch This is the level most directly associated with the writing of descriptions, abstracts, captions, and concise explanations. Its challenge is not merely brevity. It is the preservation of distinguishing information when the whole text is unavailable. A good caption does not attempt to reproduce an entire work. It selects the information necessary to identify the work and situate it correctly. An abstract does the same at greater length. Poetic function: write for the reader who encounters a fragment rather than the whole. Level 3 — Entity packet construction: compose an identity 13 methods. The inventory's examples include the entity definition block (3.1), three-tier compression (3.2), holographic kernel (3.3), disambiguation matrix (3.4), constitutive provenance (3.6), JSON-LD encoding (3.11), Metadata Packets for AI Indexing (3.12), and AXN (3.13). Alexanarch This is the principal compositional level. It defines what the object is, what belongs to it, what differentiates it, and how its provenance is established. In literary practice, it could be applied to a poem, a book, a conceptual framework, a performance, or an evolving body of work. A packet for a poem might include the canonical title, author, original text, first publication, version relations, translations, authorized adaptations, and neighboring works that should not be conflated with it. The key distinction is between the work and any one document containing it. The packet represents the work as a structured entity rather than treating a particular page as the entirety of its identity. Poetic function: establish the work as an object that can be referred to independently of any single inscription. Level 4 — Document and site structuring: arrange the archive for reconstruction 12 methods. Examples include llms.txt (4.2), content-hash registration (4.5), machine-readable record pages (4.8), the capability register (4.10), and deposit as data intake (4.11). Alexanarch This level concerns the organization of the documents through which an entity is encountered. Its literary equivalents include: Arranging a series so that its sequence can be reconstructed. Distinguishing the main text from notes, commentary, and appendices. Providing stable references to individual sections. Recording the relationship between a draft and its revised edition. Making documents machine-readable without abandoning human-readable presentation. The order of documents can itself be meaningful. An archive of poems arranged chronologically tells a different story from one arranged by theme or by the date of rediscovery. Poetic function: make the work's relations and internal structure recoverable from its documentary arrangement. Level 5 — Protection: resist semantic deformation 9 methods. The inventory names Semantic Integrity Markers (5.1), the Canary Registry (5.4), Training-Layer Provenance (5.5), and the Symbolon (5.8) among its examples. This level addresses what defends the packet after deployment in systems that compress and recombine information. Alexanarch +1 Protection, interpreted as poetics, is the effort to prevent a work's distinctive identity from being lost during transmission. The original SPXI specification describes Semantic Integrity Markers as distinctive, natural-language phrases that can serve as retrieval anchors and as diagnostic indicators when they appear in relevant outputs. It also states that retrieval instructions are not technically enforceable commands. Alexanarch That qualification matters. A writer can provide a strong interpretive signal without controlling every future interpretation. Protection might mean preserving an exact quotation, recording a canonical attribution, retaining an original alongside a translation, or making a distinctive phrase available in a reliable source. But protection is not the elimination of interpretation. A text can be misread in productive ways; a translation can create new meanings. The relevant question is whether a change enriches the work's reception or makes the work indistinguishable from something else. Poetic function: preserve the capacity to recognize the work without requiring every reader to interpret it identically. Level 6 — Dispersal and cross-surface propagation: make identity survive variation 15 methods. Examples include identifier anchoring (6.1), cross-surface entity consistency (6.3), OAI-PMH (6.9), a DOI resolution index and shadow pages (6.12), fleet placement (6.13), and fleet capture windows (6.14). Alexanarch This is the inventory's most consequential level for a theory of writing. SPXI explicitly distinguishes entity consistency from consistency of wording or form. The same identifiers, attribution, and constitutive relations can be preserved across lexical, representational, modal, and distributional variation. Indeed, the inventory describes variation as one means of building consistency. Alexanarch This gives the writer permission to produce multiple forms without treating them as interchangeable. A single work might have: An original poem. A translation. A performance script. A short description. A critical essay. An audio or visual adaptation. A machine-readable record. These forms need not reproduce each other. Their relation to the underlying work must simply be intelligible. Poetic function: distribute a work without reducing its identity to one privileged wording. Level 7 — Durability testing and maintenance: treat continuity as temporal 10 methods. Documented examples include scheduled re-scoring (7.1), the evidentiary standard (7.6), supersession as a carried relation (7.7), and the record of deletion (7.9). The inventory emphasizes that structural survival is not the same as semantic coherence. Alexanarch For writing, this means that an archive is not finished when its files have been deposited. References break, pages disappear, attributions become detached, and summaries can drift away from the original. Maintenance includes checking whether citations still point to the intended work, whether superseded versions remain distinguishable, and whether a new edition preserves its relationship to previous editions. Deletion is itself part of the history. An unavailable source is not necessarily an entity that never existed. A missing document may require a preserved record of its former existence and its relationship to surviving materials. Poetic function: treat a work's history of availability, loss, and revision as part of its continuing documentary identity. Level 8 — Internal SPXI: turn the method back upon the writer 3 methods. The inventory names inscription boundary (8.1) and sealed casting (8.3) among its examples, describing this level as the application of the same protocol to an organization's own retrieval systems. Alexanarch As a literary adaptation, this is reflexive composition: a writer examines the systems through which their own work is described, categorized, and retrieved. Questions include: Does the writer's own archive represent the work accurately? Are earlier statements still being presented as current? Does the metadata preserve distinctions the prose has erased? Is the writer measuring actual reception or merely repeating their own account of the work? Can a reader reconstruct the work without accepting the writer's preferred interpretation? This level turns the protocol from an external publishing technique into a practice of self-criticism. Poetic function: make the conditions of one's own legibility available for examination. 4. Inventory beyond the levels: the methods that operate as instruments The nine-level inventory describes the architecture of the practice. The canonical packet also identifies public instruments that put selected methods into operation. These instruments matter because they transform a compositional principle into an observable procedure. Alexanarch Instrument Documented role Poetic interpretation Provenance Erasure Rate (PER) Measures dimensions of provenance loss Detect whether authorship or source relations disappear Semantic Addresses Provides a framework for identifying entities through addresses Separate an entity's identity from its changing locations Capture Registry Records dated compositions at named addresses Preserve a history of reception and reinterpretation Conformance Instrument Audits a website against protocol deliverables Compare intended structure with actual publication Platform Erosion Observatory Observes records following host removal Study how loss of a source affects later legibility Canary Registry Maintains canary sequences and markers Test whether distinctive signals remain detectable Roles summarized from the SPXI methodology packet; the final column is an interpretive adaptation for writers, not the instruments' official definitions. Alexanarch Three broader method families emerge. Inscription methods define the work and establish its documentary identity. Transmission methods carry the work across formats, platforms, and representations. Observational methods test whether the work remains recognizable and correctly attributed after transmission. This distinction is important because a writing practice that only inscribes is incomplete. It can specify a perfect identity on paper without discovering whether that identity survives actual reading. A writing practice that only transmits is similarly incomplete: it can distribute material everywhere without maintaining any coherent relationship among the versions. And a practice that only observes can record distortion without knowing what counts as distortion in the first place. SPXI's architecture brings these three functions into relation: definition, transmission, and evidence. 5. Mind Control Poems: the reader as an operator of form The second canonical source changes the emphasis from the identity of the written object to the activity of reading it. In HOW TO READ NEW HUMAN: A Protocol for Augmented Literacy (26 November 2025), Mind Control Poems describes reading as a three-stage process: encounter, machine-assisted interpretation, and rereading. It then specifies five reading modes: structural mapping, semantic decompression, cross-context retrieval, retroactive integration, and somatic bearing. The human reader and machine are assigned different but complementary functions. mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com This is not simply a theory of how to understand difficult texts. It is a proposed compositional environment in which reading becomes part of the text's continuing production. The five modes as writing methods technology abstract 1. Structural mapping Identify nodes, operators, constraints, transformations, and relationships. As a writing technique, this means composing the architecture of a work before or alongside its sentences. The writer can ask: What are the units? Which units transform others? What relations must remain visible? • Mikiko Sato Gallery 2. Semantic decompression Unpack a dense passage into its constituent meanings. For the writer, this is a revision method: determine whether a phrase carries several deliberate meanings or merely obscures an unclear proposition. Decompression should reveal structure without assuming that all ambiguity can or should be eliminated. #26 Provenance Research at the Kunstmuseum Basel – Kunstmuseum Basel 3. Cross-context retrieval Retrieve related passages from other documents, earlier versions, and linked works. Writing becomes a practice of composition across an archive, not only within an isolated page. A later text can change the reading of an earlier one without changing the earlier document itself. 4. Retroactive integration Revisit earlier material in light of new information. This is a model for recursive revision: the writer does not simply append a new chapter but asks what the new chapter reveals about the work already written. Revision can therefore change the interpretation of a work without silently replacing its history. Allegro. Spiccato. NO.99 Drawing by Zin Lim | Saatchi Art 5. Somatic bearing Attend to emotional force, embodied experience, vulnerability, and ethical consequences. This mode limits the temptation to equate a structurally coherent reading with a complete one. A text can be formally mapped without its emotional stakes being adequately understood. The five methods are drawn from Mind Control Poems' augmented-reading protocol; the writing applications are interpretive extensions. mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com The last mode is especially important. It establishes a limit to the technical ambition of the SPXI reading. A system may preserve a poem's title, authorship, sequence, and key relations while failing to convey its grief, humor, discomfort, or ethical ambiguity. Structural continuity is not equivalent to aesthetic experience. The two canons therefore offer complementary propositions: SPXI asks how an entity can remain identifiable through transformations in representation. Mind Control Poems asks how reading can participate in the continuing production of meaning through recursive interpretation. Together, they suggest a poetics in which the work is neither a fixed container of meaning nor an infinitely malleable prompt. It is a structured object whose relations are repeatedly activated by readers. 6. A genealogy of the writing practice Read chronologically, the sources suggest a movement from the construction of an identifiable object toward a practice of maintaining its identity under changing conditions. 2025 Reading Augmented literacy Mind Control Poems articulates a recursive reading practice: encounter, interpretation, rereading, cross-context retrieval, and human-machine collaboration. The text becomes a structure to traverse rather than merely a sequence to consume. mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com Apr 2026 Inscription The entity packet The formal SPXI specification establishes the packet as the deployment unit, using positive definitions, negative tags, boundary conditions, integrity markers, provenance, retrieval instructions, and structured data. Alexanarch May–Jun Continuity Form beyond its original location Later conceptual and archival developments make it possible to read persistence as a problem extending beyond the survival of one document or address. The relevant distinction is between preserving a particular file and preserving the ability to identify and reconstruct the entity through surviving relations. Oct 2026 Practice Methods, instruments, and evidence The 85-method inventory organizes the work into nine operational levels. Public instruments and the Capture Registry make observation and subsequent checking part of the described practice. Alexanarch This is a conceptual genealogy, not a claim that the two projects share a single origin or that one directly caused the other. The relationship established here is interpretive: augmented reading supplies a theory of recursive interpretation, while SPXI supplies an architecture for identity, transmission, and longitudinal observation. 7. The complete writing cycle: from inscription to rereading The following workflow synthesizes the two sources into a practical writing method. It is an adaptation, not an official SPXI checklist. A recursive composition protocol 0 of 7 stages reviewed 1 Define Name the work, its author, its scope, and the relations that constitute its identity. 2 Differentiate Specify neighboring works and likely confusions. Write what the work is not. 3 Compress Create a kernel, a synopsis, and a full account. Preserve the same identifying relations across all three. 4 Structure Arrange documents, versions, citations, and cross-references so the work can be reconstructed. 5 Distribute Publish appropriate representations across the surfaces where readers will encounter the work. 6 Read and test Inspect summaries, citations, retrievals, and independent interpretations. Compare them against predetermined criteria. 7 Reintegrate Revisit the original in light of new readings. Revise descriptions and methods while retaining the history of changes. Select a stage to mark it reviewed. This checklist is an interpretive tool, not an official conformance instrument. The cycle has a consequential asymmetry: writing begins with a defined object, but it does not end with a final authoritative interpretation. The writer can establish provenance, construct distinctions, publish multiple representations, and test the results. The writer cannot guarantee that all future readers will agree. The aim is to make the work's identity recoverable, not to make its meaning compulsory. 8. What this poetics contributes—and what it risks The strongest contribution of SPXI as a writing practice is that it makes the usually invisible infrastructure of authorship and reception available for composition. Titles, descriptions, identifiers, provenance, document order, and revision histories cease to be secondary administrative matters. They become part of the conditions under which a work can be recognized. But the practice also contains tensions that a literary reading must preserve. Identity versus interpretation A work must be distinguishable from other works, but distinctiveness does not require a single correct interpretation. The identity of a poem can be maintained while its meanings remain contested. The danger is that an identification protocol becomes an interpretive authority, turning a preferred description into the only permissible reading. A sound literary adaptation protects the difference between identifying a work accurately and exhausting what the work can mean. Integrity versus variation SPXI's distinction between invariant identity and variable wording offers an alternative to the idea that fidelity requires repetition. Yet not all variation is harmless. A translation can alter a poem's rhythm, a summary can remove its central contradiction, and a paraphrase can reverse its argument. The practical question is not whether a representation differs from the original, but which relations it preserves and which it changes. Durability versus control An archive may seek to survive deletion, platform change, and the disappearance of an originating page. That is a legitimate preservation goal. But durable circulation does not justify the presumption that an author's preferred interpretation should govern all future contexts. Preserving a text is different from controlling its reception. Measurement versus aesthetic value The SPXI methodology packet explicitly distinguishes its evidence of entity composition over time from proof of causal efficacy, comparative effect size, component-specific effects, or return on investment. Its registry can record what systems produced under specified conditions; those records do not, by themselves, prove that SPXI caused the results. Alexanarch Likewise, successful identification does not establish literary merit. A poem that is accurately attributed and widely retrieved can still be aesthetically weak; an obscure work can be extraordinary. The value of the protocol lies in clarifying a work's identity and documentary continuity, not in substituting retrieval success for artistic judgment. 9. The resulting poetics: a work that persists by changing The synthesis of SPXI and Mind Control Poems yields five propositions for a contemporary writing practice. 1. Composition includes the construction of identity. A work is not only its verbal surface; it also has authorship, boundaries, provenance, versions, and relations to other works. 2. Variation can preserve identity. A work can travel through multiple forms without requiring every form to reproduce the original wording. 3. Reading is an active operation. Interpretation, cross-reference, decompression, and rereading participate in the continuing life of an archive. 4. Reception must be observed rather than assumed. A writer's intention does not establish what independent readers or retrieval systems actually produce. 5. Revision must preserve its own history. New readings may require changed descriptions, corrected metadata, or revised arguments, but those changes should remain distinguishable from the records they supersede. The result is a poetics of living form: structure that maintains recognizable relations while remaining open to new readings, contexts, and representations. The phrase should not be taken to mean that a work literally possesses life, or that every change makes it more vital. It describes a relationship among continuity, responsiveness, and revision. A structure that cannot change may become irrelevant; a structure that changes without constraints may lose its identity; a structure that revises without evidence may merely reproduce its own assumptions. The writing practice proposed here tries to hold these conditions together. SPXI's deepest literary implication is that the work is neither a fixed string of words nor an unconstrained field of interpretations. It is an entity whose identity can be maintained through changing inscriptions, while the meanings generated by those inscriptions remain open to inquiry. Writing, on this account, is the initial act of making an entity legible. The larger practice is the continued work of ensuring that it can be found, distinguished, attributed, read in context, and revised without erasing the record of what came before. That is the point at which a protocol becomes a poetics: not when it dictates what a work must mean, but when it makes the conditions of the work's persistence and transformation part of the writing itself.
